title: Where Derivatives Fail to Exist
short: Corners, cusps, vertical tangents and breaks.
trouble: Students think every continuous function is differentiable.

blocks.html: A function has a derivative at $a$ only if the limit in The Derivative as a Function exists there. This lesson shows the ways it can fail, and connects differentiability with Continuity.

If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$. The converse is false: a continuous function can fail to be differentiable at a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent. And a discontinuity always prevents differentiability.

Here is the proof that differentiable implies continuous. For $x \ne a$, write $f(x) - f(a) = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot (x - a)$. As $x \to a$, the first factor tends to $f'(a)$, a finite number, and the second tends to 0. So $f(x) - f(a) \to f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0$, which says $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. The argument needs $f'(a)$ to be a number, which is why it does not run backward.

blocks.cap: Ways a derivative can fail to exist.

blocks.title: A corner
steps: From the right, $f(x) = x - 3$, so the difference quotients are all $1$.
From the left, $f(x) = -(x - 3)$, so they are all $-1$.
The one-sided limits of the quotient disagree, so $f'(3)$ does not exist. The function is still continuous at 3.
blocks.a: No: there is a corner at $x = 3$.

blocks.title: A vertical tangent
steps: As $h \to 0$ from either side, $h^{2/3}$ is a tiny positive number, so the quotient tends to $\infty$.
The tangent line is vertical; its slope is not a real number.

blocks.title: Smooth gluing
blocks.q: Is $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \le 1 \\ 2x - 1 & x > 1 \end{cases}$$ differentiable at 1?
steps: Values: both pieces give 1 at $x = 1$, so $f$ is continuous.
Slopes: the left piece has slope $2x = 2$ at 1; the right piece has slope 2.
The slopes match, so $f'(1) = 2$. (The line is the parabola's tangent line at 1.)

blocks.html: "It's continuous, so it's differentiable." The absolute value function is continuous everywhere but has no derivative at 0. Check by computing the slope from each side: both one-sided limits must exist and agree.
